extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy; policymakers and historians of commerce
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and practical principles for assessing when joint-stock companies succeed or fail, when monopoly/exclusive privileges are defensible, and which kinds of trade are suitable for the joint-stock form.

rubrics_metrics.name: managerial_interest_vs_ownership_structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Directors who manage other people's money will not watch it with the same anxious vigilance as partners in a private copartnery; large dispersed ownership tends to produce negligence and profusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original text: "The directors of such companies, however, being the managers rather of other people’s money than of their own, it cannot well be expected that they should watch over it with the same anxious vigilance with which the partners in a private copartnery frequently watch over their own. Like the stewards of a rich man, they are apt to consider attention to small matters as not for their master’s honour... Negligence and profusion, therefore, must always prevail, more or less, in the management of the affairs of such a company." Use ownership concentration (few proprietors, moderate capital) as an indicator of closer vigilance; widely dispersed proprietorship and immense capital increase risk of mismanagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: need_for_exclusive_privilege_for_foreign_trade
rubrics_metrics.description: Joint-stock companies for foreign trade have seldom been able to maintain competition against private adventurers without an exclusive privilege; without monopoly they commonly mismanage the trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original text: "It is upon this account, that joint-stock companies for foreign trade have seldom been able to maintain the competition against private adventurers. They have, accordingly, very seldom succeeded without an exclusive privilege; and frequently have not succeeded with one. Without an exclusive privilege, they have commonly mismanaged the trade. With an exclusive privilege, they have both mismanaged and confined it." Assess whether a company’s foreign-trade operations depend on an enforced monopoly; absence of monopoly usually implies failure to compete with private traders.

rubrics_metrics.name: legal_confirmation_of_charters_and_exclusive_rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a company's exclusive charter is legally confirmed (e.g., by act of parliament) affects the real exclusivity of its trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Royal African company and Hudson’s Bay company had charters not confirmed by act of parliament and thus faced openness of trade; South Sea and United East India Company had privileges confirmed by act of parliament. Evaluate the legal basis for exclusivity (charter vs statutory confirmation) when judging the strength of a company's monopoly.

rubrics_metrics.name: temporary_monopoly_as_compensation_for_risk
rubrics_metrics.description: A temporary monopoly may be justified to recompense merchants who, at their own risk and expense, establish a new trade with a remote nation; it is analogous to temporary patents or copyrights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original text: "When a company of merchants undertake, at their own risk and expense, to establish a new trade with some remote and barbarous nation, it may not be unreasonable to incorporate them into a joint-stock company, and to grant them, in case of their success, a monopoly of the trade for a certain number of years... But upon the expiration of the term, the monopoly ought certainly to determine..." Use duration-limited monopoly as an acceptable incentive; perpetual monopoly is condemned.

rubrics_metrics.name: opposition_to_perpetual_monopoly
rubrics_metrics.description: Perpetual monopolies are unjustified because they tax other subjects by raising prices and excluding them from profitable business; upon expiry forts should transfer to government and trade be opened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original text: "By a perpetual monopoly, all the other subjects of the state are taxed very absurdly in two different ways... first, by the high price of goods... secondly, by their total exclusion from a branch of business..." Policy implication: monopolies should be time-limited and their territorial assets handed to state control upon expiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: suitability_of_trade_to_joint-stock_form
rubrics_metrics.description: Only trades whose operations can be reduced to a routine or uniform method are likely to be carried on successfully by joint-stock companies without exclusive privileges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: banking; insurance (fire, sea risk, capture in war); making and maintaining a navigable canal; water supply for a great city. Rationale: routine operations can be reduced to strict rules and managed by boards following established procedure; assess the degree to which a trade is routinizable.

rubrics_metrics.name: banking_and_rule_based_operations_fit_joint_stock
rubrics_metrics.description: Banking practices, though somewhat abstruse, can be reduced to strict rules; joint-stock constitution tends to make companies tenacious of established rules and thus well suited to banking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original text: "Such companies, therefore, seem extremely well fitted for this trade. The principal banking companies in Europe, accordingly, are joint-stock companies..." Evaluate whether the trade permits governance by fixed rules and penalties for deviation.

rubrics_metrics.name: insurance_as_joint_stock-friendly
rubrics_metrics.description: Insurance (valuation of risk from fire, sea loss or capture) admits of gross estimation making it reasonably reducible to rule and therefore suitable for joint-stock operation without monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original text: "The value of the risk... admits, however, of such a gross estimation, as renders it, in some degree, reducible to strict rule and method." Consider whether risk-evaluation for the line of business is amenable to actuarial/statistical rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: private_adventurer_advantage_in_non-routine_trades
rubrics_metrics.description: Trades requiring constant vigilance, dexterity, judgment, adaptation to variations in demand and competition are better conducted by private adventurers than by joint-stock companies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original text: "To buy in one market, in order to sell with profit in another, when there are many competitors in both... is a species of warfare... which can scarce ever be conducted successfully, without such an unremitting exertion of vigilance and attention as cannot long be expected from the directors of a joint-stock company." Evaluate how much agility and local judgment the trade demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: effects_of_large_divided_capital_on_mismanagement
rubrics_metrics.description: An immense capital divided among an immense number of proprietors naturally predisposes the company to folly, negligence, and profusion in management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: South Sea company had immense divided capital and consequent mismanagement and stock-jobbing. Use dispersion of capital and size of proprietor base as risk factors for speculative or negligent behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: corporate_governance_reforms_have_limited_capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutional changes (raising voting qualification, lengthening director terms, rotation, council/governor-general in India, new courts) may improve steadiness and dignity but cannot make proprietors deeply interested in the empire’s prosperity; thus such reforms have limited effect on true competence to govern territories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original text: various enacted changes (higher vote qualification, four-year directors, governor-general with council, new supreme court) expected to improve governance but Smith argues: "it seems impossible, by any alterations, to render those courts, in any respect, fit to govern... because the greater part of their members must always have too little interest in the prosperity of that empire..." Use reforms as partial mitigations but not cures for principal-agent indifference.

rubrics_metrics.name: corporate_possession_of_forts_confers_war_peace_powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The right to possess forts and garrisons in distant countries is necessarily connected with the right to make peace and war in those countries; joint-stock companies exercising these powers have often done so unjustly and cruelly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original text: "With the right of possessing forts and garrisons in distant and barbarous countries is necessarily connected the right of making peace and war... How unjustly, how capriciously, how cruelly, they have commonly exercised it, is too well known from recent experience." Consider political and moral fitness before granting territorial/military authority to commercial corporations.

rubrics_metrics.name: perverse_incentives_of_proprietors_and_servants
rubrics_metrics.description: Proprietors often care more for influence (appointments, patronage) than for dividends or the prosperity of the empire; servants may be tempted to embezzle or plunder when surplus is available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original text: "Frequently a man...is willing to purchase...share...merely for the influence which he expects to acquire by a vote... he frequently cares little about the dividend... About the prosperity of the great empire... he seldom cares at all... It might be more agreeable to the company, that their own servants and dependants should either the pleasure of wasting, or the profit of embezzling..." When evaluating governance, examine incentives for votes, appointments, and tolerance of malversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: historical_evidence_of_joint_stock_failures
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical/historical record indicates many joint-stock companies for foreign trade established since 1600 failed from mismanagement, even when they had exclusive privileges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference: Abbe Morellet’s list of fifty-five companies, with caveats. Use historical failure rates as part of risk assessment for proposing new corporate monopolies or granting state-like powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: external_financial_obligations_and_dividend_constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Government loans, annuities, bond-debts, and agreements to remit revenues to the public can constrain a company’s dividends and change managers’ incentives, sometimes worsening stewardship rather than improving it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: East India Company’s agreements to pay government £400,000/year and parliamentary resolutions about reserving revenue changed incentives: "But if the company were bad stewards... they were surely not likely to be better when three-fourths of them were to belong to other people..." Evaluate how public financial obligations influence corporate behavior and stewardship incentives.
